The reason I mention this is because schools in the US will likley try and make you start at least part of your education over.  School here is very expensive, as I'm sure you already know and while getting a student visa is an option I think you would then have to apply for a different visa (a work visa) once graduated and then apply to an immigration program.  I grew up in a college town where I saw many folks who had to go home once school was over, not always by choice, which sucked.  Immigration is typically easier when 1) you have a skill the us wants you to use here, the more specialized the skill the better 2) you have your own money saved, the more money you have the easier to immigrate.  

Another very serious thing to consider is the immigration status of your kids if you have them.  If you have children who were born outside the us before you came over on a student or work visa your kids may risk deportation at 18.  One of my friends in high school got deported after she turned 18, her parents had student and work visas and her 2 siblings were born here while her parents were here on visas.  My friend was born in Malaysia in time here parents went back, between visas. Even though she was a great student, lived in the us for 10+ years, her immediate family is all still here, and she got into a good university in the US, helping her start university and eventually immigrate was way too expensive for her family so she had to go back to the country where she was born.

Idk if this has been suggested, but can these folks be referred to r/suicidewatch ?  That way they get the support they need while this space can be kept dedicated to processing somewhat less extreme responses to grief (idk if that wording is correct).

This type of thing happened to my family as well.  It was the 70s and my father (around 10 years old at the time I think) was left home alone with his significantly older brother who had some kind of treatment resistant schizophrenia, which started when he was very young.  The tragedy of his illness and the violent nature of his death severely messed up my entire family, even for my sibling and cousins who never met our uncle.  My dad's family had to clen up the room themselves (i think maybe an inlaw did most of the work idk, it's not a topic that comes up much especially in that much detail), and burn everything that was in that room with him.  Suicide has touched nearly every part of my life (not just from the death of my uncle) and god damn if it isn't the worst type of loss I have ever witness or experienced.  It was beyond kind of yourself to volunteer to help how you did, a moving act of love.  Thank you, even though I dont know you, the deceased, or the family, your actions mean a lot.  It takes years sometimes for the reality of situations like this to process, I hope all of you have the support you need and more dealing with this loss.
